Battleships were a more expensive option whose future role was already in doubt. This makes hull space and cost the central reasons for choosing cruisers.

evidence.note: Cruiser space and affordability as reasons for mounting early missiles, compared with the uncertain future of battleships.

segments.summary: Cruisers offered the space for early missile systems without the cost and strategic baggage of battleships.
segments.question: Was the missile cruiser a new 1950s-60s idea, or did the concept appear earlier?
segments.answerShort: It emerged with practical missiles because cruisers had the necessary space at lower cost than battleships.

segments.title: Length-to-beam ratio, hull form, and capital-ship resistance
segments.body: There is no single length-to-beam cutoff in this explanation because the shape of the underwater hull also matters. A flatter hull provides useful internal space, while sharper V-shaped sections offer another way to manage resistance as a ship gets longer. The battleship hull associated with Béarn's conversion provides the illustrated example: a sharp forward section rolls into a fuller form farther aft. Loading is part of the problem too, with a slightly lighter bow proposed to help the ship ride across waves. These choices connect hull proportions to the shape and trim of the complete vessel.

evidence.note: V-shaped and flatter sections, the illustrated Béarn battleship hull, and the effect of loading forward and aft.

segments.summary: Hull cross-section and loading affect the resistance of a long capital ship, so length-to-beam ratio alone cannot settle the design.
segments.question: At what capital-ship length-to-beam ratio does added hydrodynamic efficiency lose to the resistance of greater surface area?
segments.answerShort: The balance depends on the hull's cross-section and trim as well as its proportions; no single cutoff ratio is given.

segments.title: Why a bow-heavy ship can dig into waves
segments.body: Loading the bow more heavily is questioned because it can make the front of a ship dig into waves. Water coming aboard then pushes it farther down. A slightly lighter bow is proposed to help it rise and pass across the water. Footage of an Arleigh Burke in rough weather provides the example of a bow repeatedly going under.

evidence.note: Explanation of bow-heavy trim, water coming aboard, and an Arleigh Burke rough-weather example.

segments.summary: A slightly lighter bow can rise across waves instead of digging into them and taking water aboard.
segments.question: Would loading a battlecruiser's bow more heavily improve its behavior at high speed?
segments.answerShort: Not necessarily; a heavy bow can dig into waves and take water aboard, while a lighter bow rises more readily.

segments.title: Could Hood plane at high speed?
segments.body: A capital ship of 30,000 or 40,000 tons would need much more speed to plane than its machinery could provide. A recollected calculation for Hood puts that speed at about 90 knots. The estimate is used to distinguish a fast displacement ship from a vessel lifted into a planing condition.

evidence.note: Capital-ship displacement and a recollected estimate of roughly 90 knots for Hood to plane.

segments.summary: A recollected 90-knot estimate places planing far beyond Hood's practical speed.
segments.question: Would a battlecruiser risk planing or aquaplaning at high speed?
segments.answerShort: No; lifting such a large displacement into a plane would require a speed far beyond the ship's capability.

segments.title: How Hood's bow-wave trough could expose lower hull
segments.body: Hood's apparent exposure of lower hull is explained by the wave pattern along its side. The water rises in the bow wave and then falls in the trough behind it. That local fall can reveal plating below the main armour belt while the ship remains a displacement vessel. Battlecruisers sometimes carried a thin lower belt or omitted it to save weight, leaving less protection in that area.

evidence.note: Bow-wave crest and trough distinguished from the hull lifting, followed by battlecruisers' thin or absent lower belts.

segments.summary: The local trough behind a bow wave can expose hull below the main belt without the ship planing.
segments.question: Was Hood's lower hull exposed because its bow rose out of the water at speed?
segments.answerShort: The explanation is the trough behind the bow wave, which lowers the water locally and can expose less-protected hull.

segments.title: Could battlecruisers fight safely at flank speed?
segments.body: Battlecruisers could fight at flank speed despite the possibility that a wave trough exposed hull below the main belt. Renown's illustrated armour layout shows several layers of coverage, with a battleship expected to carry protection farther down. Turning is said to make the exposed gap more pronounced. Hitting that small, moving gap at battle ranges would nevertheless be extremely unlikely, so the vulnerability was an accepted risk. Fast battleships also experienced the wave effect, though deeper lower belts gave them more protection.

evidence.note: Renown's lower-belt layout, greater exposure during turns, the rhetorical description of a very unlikely hit, and deeper battleship protection.

segments.summary: A small moving gap below the main belt is treated as an acceptable combat risk, with battleships gaining more coverage from deeper belts.
segments.question: Did exposure below the armour belt prevent battlecruisers from fighting at flank speed?
segments.answerShort: No; exploiting the small moving gap would be very difficult, and similar wave effects also affected fast battleships.

segments.title: Battlecruiser armour, speed, and strategic tradeoffs
segments.body: An armour analogy distinguishes a dreadnought armoured cruiser, a more developed battlecruiser, a fast battleship, and a fully protected battleship by the extent of their coverage. Greater protection costs weight, and the balance remains a design problem even without naval treaties or dockyard limits. A battlecruiser's sustained cruising speed is especially useful: an advantage of four or five knots can shorten a strategic redeployment. That lets the ship reach a distant concentration or chosen target sooner. Accepting less protection is therefore a decision about the jobs the ship must perform and the risks those jobs justify. The closing lance-and-shield comparison expresses that strategic distinction, with the battlecruiser valued for reaching and striking a target.

evidence.note: Graduated armour analogy, treaty and dockyard constraints, a four- or five-knot cruising-speed advantage, and the strategic risks accepted for faster redeployment.

segments.summary: A battlecruiser's sustained cruising speed can justify accepting less armour because it makes strategic redeployment faster.
